Its coefficients are Hölder after the $C^{1,1}$ bound; interior elliptic regularity and differentiation make the graph smooth.\n\nIf this smooth MOTS touches $S$, their one-sided difference satisfies a linear elliptic equation with bounded coefficients. The strong comparison principle gives local coincidence. The contact set is thus open and closed in connected $S$, so the cut contains $S$. Its full area is already $A$, excluding additional positive-area components. If it does not touch $S$, it is a smooth compact full enclosing MOTS entirely in the interior, after filling removable pockets. This contradicts outermostness. Hence almost every cut is exactly $S$. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### A local adjoint lemma and finite-type continuation\n\nThe following version records the cosmological constant explicitly, for later use on annuli. Set $$16\\pi\\mu_{\\Lambda_{\\rm c}}\n    =R-2\\Lambda_{\\rm c}+(\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}K)^2-|K|^2,\\qquad\n 8\\pi J=\\operatorname{div}_g(K-(\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}K)g).$$\n\n\n<div id=\"eq-local-adjoint\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n\n\n**Lemma 90** (Local regularity and the full adjoint). *Let $g,K$ be smooth on a connected open three-manifold and let $\\Lambda_{\\rm c}$ be constant. Suppose locally finite moment measures $u,X$ satisfy $u\\geq|X|$, $u\\mu_{\\Lambda_{\\rm c}}+J(X)=0$, and annihilate every compact variation of $16\\pi(\\mu_{\\Lambda_{\\rm c}}+J(v))$, including the isometric-vector correction <a href=\"#eq-vector-transport\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-vector-transport\">[eq-vector-transport]</a>. Then $u,X$ are smooth and $$\\begin{aligned}\n \\operatorname{sym}\\nabla X&=-uK,\\label{eq-general-shift}\\\\\n \\Delta u+\\Lambda_{\\rm c}u\n   &=-\\operatorname{div}_g(K(X,\\cdot)^\\sharp),\\label{eq-general-lapse}\\\\\n \\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}u\n   &=u(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}-\\Lambda_{\\rm c}g+\\tau_KK-2K^2)\n       -\\mathcal L_XK+8\\pi X_{(i}J_{j)},\\qquad \\tau_K=\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}K.\n       \\label{eq-general-full-lapse}\n\\end{aligned}$$ Their full first jet satisfies a homogeneous linear first-order system with smooth coefficients depending on $g,K,\\Lambda_{\\rm c}$. A jet vanishing at one point vanishes everywhere. If the moments are nonzero, then $u>0$ everywhere.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-eq-local-adjoint\"><summary>Proof of stmt-eq-local-adjoint</summary>\n\n*Proof.* For a pure tensor variation $P$, integration of momentum by parts gives the distributional coefficient $$2\\big[u(\\tau_Kg-K)-\\operatorname{sym}\\nabla X\n                         +(\\operatorname{div}X)g\\big].$$ Its trace gives $\\operatorname{div}X=-u\\tau_K$, and substitution gives <a href=\"#eq-general-shift\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-general-shift\">[eq-general-shift]</a>. A simultaneous conformal test $(4\\psi g,2\\psi K)$, using complementarity to cancel its background scaling term, gives $$8\\langle u,(-\\Delta-\\Lambda_{\\rm c})\\psi\\rangle\n       +8\\langle X,K(\\nabla\\psi,\\cdot)\\rangle=0.$$ This is <a href=\"#eq-general-lapse\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-general-lapse\">[eq-general-lapse]</a>. Diverging the shift equation and using its trace gives $$\\Delta X_j+\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{jk}X^k\n  =(\\tau_K\\delta_j{}^i-2K_j{}^i)\\nabla_i u\n       +u(\\nabla_j\\tau_K-2\\nabla^iK_{ij}).\n \\label{eq-vector-elliptic}$$ Together with the lapse equation this is an elliptic system with diagonal scalar-Laplacian principal part and smooth first-order couplings. Measures belong locally to a negative Sobolev space. The local elliptic estimate on nested compact cutoffs improves their Sobolev order by one, because the couplings have at most one derivative. Iteration and Sobolev embedding yield smoothness.\n\n\n\nFor completeness, the metric equation is computed next. Put $P_K=K-\\tau_Kg$. The compact constraint pairing is the variation of $$\\int\\big[u(R-2\\Lambda_{\\rm c}+\\tau_K^2-|K|^2)\n                  +2X^i\\nabla^j(P_K)_{ij}\\big]\\,dV_g$$ together with $-8\\pi\\int H(X,J^\\sharp)\\,dV_g$. The latter is exactly the vector-transport correction. Changing the fixed background volume density to the varying one adds zero, since its background integrand is $16\\pi(u\\mu_{\\Lambda_{\\rm c}}+J(X))=0$. Integrating the shift term once gives $-\\int P_K^{ij}(\\mathcal L_Xg)_{ij}\\,dV_g$. At fixed covariant $K$, contravariant $X$, and $u$, use $$\\begin{split}\n R'&=-\\langle\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}},H\\rangle+\\nabla^i\\nabla^jH_{ij}\n                                  -\\Delta\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}H,\\\\\n \\tau_K'&=-K^{ij}H_{ij},\\qquad\n (|K|^2)'=-2(K^2)^{ij}H_{ij},\\\\\n (P_K^{ij})'&=-H^i{}_aK^{aj}-H^j{}_aK^{ia}\n                    +(K^{ab}H_{ab})g^{ij}+\\tau_KH^{ij},\\\\\n (\\mathcal L_Xg)'&=\\mathcal L_XH,\\qquad\n (dV_g)'=\\tfrac12(\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}H)dV_g.\n \\end{split}$$ Integration of $\\mathcal L_XH$ and collection of coefficients gives $$\\begin{aligned}\n 0={}&\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}u-(\\Delta u)g-u\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}+2u(K^2-\\tau_KK)\n      +\\frac u2(R-2\\Lambda_{\\rm c}+\\tau_K^2-|K|^2)g \\notag\\\\\n &+\\mathcal L_XK-(\\operatorname{div}X)K\n       -\\big(X(\\tau_K)+K^{ab}\\nabla_aX_b\\big)g\n       -8\\pi X_{(i}J_{j)}.\n \\label{eq-unsimplified-metric}\n\\end{aligned}$$ The shift equation gives $$\\operatorname{div}X=-u\\tau_K,\\quad\n K^{ab}\\nabla_aX_b=-u|K|^2,\\quad\n \\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}(\\mathcal L_XK)=X(\\tau_K)-2u|K|^2.$$ Taking the trace of <a href=\"#eq-unsimplified-metric\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-unsimplified-metric\">[eq-unsimplified-metric]</a> and using complementarity yields $$\\Delta u+X(\\tau_K)\n   =\\frac u2(R+\\tau_K^2+|K|^2-4\\Lambda_{\\rm c}).\n \\label{eq-trace-identity}$$ Substitution gives <a href=\"#eq-general-full-lapse\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-general-full-lapse\">[eq-general-full-lapse]</a>.\n\n\nTo exhibit finite type, write $B_{ij}=\\nabla_{(i}X_{j)}=-uK_{ij}$. Commuting covariant derivatives gives $$\\begin{split}\n \\nabla_i\\nabla_jX_k\n ={}&\\nabla_iB_{jk}+\\nabla_jB_{ik}-\\nabla_kB_{ij}\\\\\n &+\\tfrac12\\big([\\nabla_i,\\nabla_j]X_k\n       -[\\nabla_i,\\nabla_k]X_j-[\\nabla_j,\\nabla_k]X_i\\big).\n \\end{split}$$ All commutators are curvature times $X$. Derivatives of $B$ use only $u,du$ and the first derivatives of $K$. Equation <a href=\"#eq-general-full-lapse\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-general-full-lapse\">[eq-general-full-lapse]</a> similarly expresses the Hessian of $u$ in first jets. Therefore, for $\\mathcal J=(u,X,\\nabla u,\\nabla X)$, $$\\nabla\\mathcal J=\\mathcal A(g,K,\\Lambda_{\\rm c})\\,\\mathcal J\n \\label{eq-finite-type}$$ for a smooth bundle-valued linear coefficient. ODE uniqueness along paths proves continuation. At a zero of $u\\geq0$, $du=0$; domination $|X|\\leq u$ also gives $X=dX=0$. Nonzero moments consequently have positive lapse everywhere. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"eq-jet-compactness\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n**Lemma 91** (Compactness of normalized adjoint jets). *Suppose smooth coefficients in Lemma <a href=\"#eq-local-adjoint\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-local-adjoint\">90</a> converge on compact subsets of a connected open manifold, and nonzero causal adjoints are defined on an exhaustion containing a fixed point $p$. Normalize their full first jets at $p$ to have norm one. A subsequence converges smoothly on compact sets to a nonzero causal adjoint for the limiting coefficients. The same conclusion holds for a parameter family on a fixed open manifold.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-eq-jet-compactness\"><summary>Proof of stmt-eq-jet-compactness</summary>\n\n*Proof.* The jet at $p$ cannot be zero by continuation. On any fixed compact set, a finite family of coordinate neighborhoods and paths from $p$ has bounded lengths and uniformly bounded coefficients in <a href=\"#eq-finite-type\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-finite-type\">[eq-finite-type]</a>. Grönwall’s Inequality gives uniform first-jet bounds there. The equations and local elliptic estimates give bounds of every order on smaller compact sets. Diagonal compactness gives the limit. Its jet at $p$ still has norm one, and causality is a closed pointwise condition. Lemma <a href=\"#eq-local-adjoint\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-local-adjoint\">90</a> supplies positive limiting lapse. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### Boundary atoms and hyperbolic normalization\n\nBy Lemma <a href=\"#eq-area-concentration\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-area-concentration\">89</a>, the area term in <a href=\"#eq-multiplier-identity\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-multiplier-identity\">[eq-multiplier-identity]</a> is $c\\,a'_S(H)$. Thus compact interior tests have zero pairing, and Lemma <a href=\"#eq-local-adjoint\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-local-adjoint\">90</a>, with $\\Lambda_{\\rm c}=-3$, applies. It gives <a href=\"#eq-shift\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-shift\">[eq-shift]</a>–<a href=\"#eq-full-lapse\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-full-lapse\">[eq-full-lapse]</a> in the interior.\n\n\n<div id=\"eq-normalization-lemma\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n**Lemma 92** (One-sided continuation and normalization). *The moment fields extend smoothly to $S$, their original measure moments have no part supported on $S$, and they satisfy <a href=\"#eq-end-normalization\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-end-normalization\">[eq-end-normalization]</a>. In particular they are nonzero and their lapse is positive in the interior.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-eq-normalization-lemma\"><summary>Proof of stmt-eq-normalization-lemma</summary>\n\n*Proof.* In a smooth normal collar of $S$, the coefficient in <a href=\"#eq-finite-type\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-finite-type\">[eq-finite-type]</a> is smooth up to the face. Solve its linear ODE down each collar segment from a fixed interior surface. Smooth dependence on its footpoint gives a smooth extension; ODE uniqueness identifies it with the original field in the collar.\n\nSubtract integration by parts of these smooth interior fields from the compact multiplier identity. Take a metric variation whose value and full first jet vanish on $S$, and set the tensor variation to zero. All area, expansion and integrated boundary terms vanish. The remaining boundary scalar moment tests $-\\partial_\\nu^2\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}_SH$, which is arbitrary, by choosing a prescribed $s^2$ tangential trace in collar coordinates. Momentum and frame terms involve only lower jets and are zero. Thus the scalar moment has no boundary part. Its domination of the vector moment eliminates that part as well.\n\nWe next derive end behavior without imposing growth on the measures. Express the first-jet system in a $b$-parallel radial frame, with $\\eta=\\operatorname{arsinh}r$. At $(b,0)$ its lapse system is $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_bu=ub$ and its shift system is hyperbolic Killing transport. Their radial propagators have norm at most $C e^{|\\eta-\\eta'|}$. This follows directly from the $2$-by-$2$ blocks $y''=y$ and the constant blocks, or from the ambient linear functions and Lorentz generators on the hyperboloid. The actual coefficient differs by $O(e^{-\\tau\\eta})$; only two metric derivatives and one tensor derivative occur. Variation of constants gives $$e^{-\\eta}|\\mathcal J(\\eta)|\n \\leq C+C\\int_{\\eta_0}^{\\eta}\n        e^{-\\tau s}e^{-s}|\\mathcal J(s)|\\,ds.$$ Grönwall therefore gives $\\mathcal J=O(r)$, uniformly in angle.\n\nThe lapse and tangential-shift radial equations now read $$y''-y=O(r^{1-\\tau}),$$ and the normal-shift derivative is $O(r^{1-\\tau})$. Variation of constants, with $3/2<\\beta<\\min\\{2,\\tau\\}$, consequently gives continuous angular coefficients $$\\begin{aligned}\n u&=r f_0(\\omega)+O(r^{1-\\beta}),&\n \\partial_{\\eta}u&=r f_0(\\omega)+O(r^{1-\\beta}),\\\\\n X_T&=r W_0(\\omega)+O(r^{1-\\beta}),&\n X^{\\nu_b}&=a_0(\\omega)+O(r^{1-\\beta}).\n\\end{aligned}$$ Convergence of the leading coefficients is uniform; no angular differentiability is required at this stage. The homogeneous $r^{-1}$ mode is included in the remainder because $\\beta<2$.\n\nUse first a conformal prototype $\\psi=r^{-3}f(\\omega)$ in the multiplier identity and integrate to a large sphere. Its interior pairing vanishes by the adjoint equations, its $S$ terms vanish, and its end-point coefficient is zero. All pairings converge: the moments grow at most as $r$, while the prototype derivatives are $O(r^{-4})+O(r^{-3-\\tau})$ or better. The sole nonvanishing boundary expression is $$-8\\int_{r=R}\n       (u\\partial_{\\nu_b}\\psi-\\psi\\partial_{\\nu_b}u)\\,dA_b.$$ Terms containing $KX\\psi$ have integrated order $O(R^{-\\tau})$; replacing $g$ by $b$ has the same vanishing order. The displayed limit is $32\\int_{\\mathbb S^2}f_0f\\,d\\omega$. The left side is $16\\pi p'_0=32\\int_{\\mathbb S^2}f\\,d\\omega$ by the defining metric flux. Arbitrary $f$ gives $f_0=1$.\n\nFor a mixed tensor prototype, the only boundary term is twice its trace-reversed stress flux against $X$. Its limit is $2\\int_{\\mathbb S^2}\\langle W_0,W\\rangle_\\sigma\\,d\\omega$, whereas its metric mass and area derivatives vanish. Hence $W_0=0$. The tangential trace of the shift equation on coordinate spheres now gives $$\\operatorname{div}_{S_R}X_T+H_{S_R}X^{\\nu_b}\n                      =O(R^{1-\\beta}).$$ Interpret this on the unit sphere. The divergence term tends to zero distributionally, since integration against a fixed test function gains the factor $R^{-1}$, and $H_{S_R}\\to2$. Thus $a_0=0$. The already uniform limits identify it pointwise.\n\nWe have obtained the value estimates in <a href=\"#eq-end-normalization\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-end-normalization\">[eq-end-normalization]</a>, since $V_0-r=O(r^{-1})$. The coupled elliptic system for $(u-V_0,X)$ has uniformly controlled unit-patch coefficients and source $O_{0,\\alpha'}(r^{1-\\tau})$. Local estimates applied to these value bounds yield the first and second derivative Hölder bounds in <a href=\"#eq-end-normalization\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-end-normalization\">[eq-end-normalization]</a>, with a smaller $\\alpha'$ if necessary. The prototype normalization makes the field nonzero; the last assertion of Lemma <a href=\"#eq-local-adjoint\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-local-adjoint\">90</a> gives $u>0$. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### Stationary curvature and free boundary variations\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-eq-normalization-lemma-2\"><summary>Proof of stmt-eq-normalization-lemma</summary>\n\n*Completion of the proof of Theorem <a href=\"#eq-causal-killing\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-causal-killing\">84</a>.* Since $u>0$, <a href=\"#eq-stationary-metric\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-stationary-metric\">[eq-stationary-metric]</a> is a smooth Lorentzian metric on the open exterior product. Its coefficients are independent of $t$, so $\\xi=\\partial_t$ is Killing. Its future normal is $n=u^{-1}(\\partial_t-X)$; the future-normal convention fixed after Equation <a href=\"#eq:setup-expansion\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq:setup-expansion\">[eq:setup-expansion]</a> gives $$\\tfrac12\\mathcal L_n g=-\\frac1{2u}\\mathcal L_Xg=K$$ by <a href=\"#eq-shift\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-shift\">[eq-shift]</a>. Thus both induced tensors are the original ones.\n\nWe verify its curvature without a spacetime existence assumption. The Gauss–Codazzi and lapse identities, obtained by differentiating the displayed metric, give for spatial slots $$\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{\\mathbf g,ij}\n =\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{g,ij}+\\tau_KK_{ij}-2(K^2)_{ij}\n       -u^{-1}\\big((\\mathcal L_XK)_{ij}+(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}u)_{ij}\\big),$$ and $$R_{\\mathbf g}=R_g+\\tau_K^2+|K|^2\n                     -2u^{-1}(\\Delta u+X(\\tau_K)).$$ Equation <a href=\"#eq-trace-identity\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-trace-identity\">[eq-trace-identity]</a> with $\\Lambda_{\\rm c}=-3$ gives $R_{\\mathbf g}=-12$. Equation <a href=\"#eq-full-lapse\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-full-lapse\">[eq-full-lapse]</a> then gives $$u(G_{\\mathbf g}-3\\mathbf g)_{ij}=-8\\pi X_{(i}J_{j)}.$$ The normal and mixed components of this tensor are the constraints, $8\\pi\\mu$ and $8\\pi J_i$. Complementarity and causality imply $$0=u\\mu+J(X)\\geq u\\mu-|J||X|\n                \\geq u(\\mu-|J|)\\geq0.$$ Where $\\mu>0$, equality forces $|X|=u$, $|J|=\\mu$, and $J=-\\mu X^\\flat/u$. Where $\\mu=0$, $J=0$. Substitution into all the normal, mixed and spatial components gives $$G_{\\mathbf g}-3\\mathbf g\n      =8\\pi\\mu u^{-2}\\xi^\\flat\\otimes\\xi^\\flat,\\qquad\n \\mu(u^2-|X|^2)=0.$$ Since the matter term is tracefree, this is exactly <a href=\"#eq-null-matter\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-null-matter\">[eq-null-matter]</a>. It allows nonzero matter on the null set; its exclusion is a separate argument in the next section.\n\nIt remains to determine the boundary data. There are no boundary constraint atoms by Lemma <a href=\"#eq-normalization-lemma\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-normalization-lemma\">92</a>, and the integration normal at $S$ is $-\\nu$. A compact pure tensor test $P$, arbitrary at the boundary, has integrated boundary term $$-2\\int_S\\big(P(X,\\nu)-X^\\nu\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}P\\big)\\,dA_g.$$ Its expansion derivative is $\\mathop{\\mathrm{tr}}_SP$. Separating mixed and tangential-trace components in <a href=\"#eq-multiplier-identity\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"eq-multiplier-identity\">[eq-multiplier-identity]</a> gives $$X_T=0,\\qquad d\\eta=2X^\\nu\\,dA_g.$$ For a compact simultaneous conformal test $(4\\psi g,2\\psi K)$, its area derivative is $4\\int_S\\psi\\,dA_g$ and its expansion derivative is $4\\partial_\\nu\\psi$. Integrating the lapse equation gives $$-4c\\int_S\\psi\\,dA_g\n =8\\int_S\\big[u\\partial_\\nu\\psi\n        -(\\partial_\\nu u+K(X,\\nu))\\psi\\big]\\,dA_g\n       -4\\int_S\\partial_\\nu\\psi\\,d\\eta .$$ The boundary value and normal derivative of $\\psi$ can be prescribed independently. They give $d\\eta=2u\\,dA_g$, $X=u\\nu$, and $\\partial_\\nu u+K(X,\\nu)=c/2=\\kappa_h$.\n\nFinally let $L_{\\rm MOTS}$ be the normal expansion linearization at $S$, with principal part $-\\Delta_S$. Extend any $s\\nu$, $s\\in C^\\infty(S)$, to a compact one-sided field $Y$ and test with $(\\mathcal L_Yg,\\mathcal L_YK)$. In the open exterior its active-ray derivative is zero: under diffeomorphism transport it differentiates a nonnegative scalar at a zero, and the difference from isometric transport is annihilated at activity. No boundary constraint measure remains. The mass derivative is zero, while the area and expansion derivatives are $\\int_SHs\\,dA_g$ and $L_{\\rm MOTS}s$. The multiplier identity therefore gives $$c\\int_SHs\\,dA_g=2\\int_SuL_{\\rm MOTS}s\\,dA_g,\\qquad\n 2L_{\\rm MOTS}^*u=cH.$$ Outer area minimization gives $H\\geq0$, by the first area variation for arbitrary nonnegative outward speeds. The nonnegative function $u|_S$ is consequently a supersolution of an elliptic operator with principal part $-\\Delta_S$. The strong minimum principle applies: after reversing the operator and subtracting a sufficiently large zeroth-order constant, the usual nonpositive zeroth-order condition holds because $u\\geq0$. On connected $S$, either $u>0$ everywhere or $u=0$ everywhere. This completes all assertions. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n### The timelike region and the regular static quotient\n\nWe now use the causal stationary field supplied by Theorem <a href=\"#eq-causal-killing\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-causal-killing\">84</a>. All geometric objects in this section are constructed from the original equality data. The logarithmic estimate below is a cosmological version of the Killing-norm calculation in (OpenAI 2026b, sec. 5.3) [[internalflat](#ref-internalflat)]; we give its proof, including the treatment of an arbitrary interior null set.\n\n\n\n\nWrite $M=\\operatorname{int}\\Omega$, and let $\\nu$ on $S$ point into $\\Omega$. We record the precise outputs of Theorem <a href=\"#eq-causal-killing\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-causal-killing\">84</a> that are used. The fields $u,X$ are smooth up to $S$, satisfy $u>0$ on $M$ and $u\\geq|X|_g$, and obey $$\\operatorname{sym}\\nabla X=-uK,\n \\qquad X|_S=u\\nu,\n \\qquad \\partial_\\nu u+K(X,\\nu)=\\kappa_h>0,\n \\label{geo-input-killing}$$ where $\\kappa_h$ is a constant. Either $u|_S>0$ everywhere or $u|_S=0$ everywhere. Writing $\\tau'$ for the exponent $\\beta$ in Theorem <a href=\"#eq-causal-killing\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"eq-causal-killing\">84</a>, with $\\tau'>3/2$, the end estimates are $$u-V_0=O_2(r^{1-\\tau'}),\\qquad X=O_2(r^{1-\\tau'}).\n \\label{geo-input-end}$$ Here and below the end estimates use the reference hyperbolic tensor norms, including their stated differentiated Hölder bounds. The stationary metric $$\\mathbf g=-u^2\\,\\mathrm dt^2+\n g_{ij}(\\,\\mathrm dx^i+X^i\\,\\mathrm dt)(\\,\\mathrm dx^j+X^j\\,\\mathrm dt)\n \\label{geo-stationary-metric}$$ on $\\mathbb R\\times M$, with $\\xi=\\partial_t$ and $N=u^2-|X|_g^2$, satisfies $$\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{\\mathbf g}=-3\\mathbf g+\n       8\\pi\\mu u^{-2}\\xi^\\flat\\otimes\\xi^\\flat,\n \\qquad \\mu N=0.\n \\label{geo-input-ricci}$$ The musical notation on $\\xi$ refers to $\\mathbf g$; spatial musical notation will always refer to $g$ unless specified otherwise.\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-static-reduction\" class=\"theorem\">\n\n\n\n\n\n**Theorem 93** (Regular static quotient). *<span id=\"geo-static-quotient\" label=\"geo-static-quotient\"></span> Under these hypotheses, $N>0$ throughout $M$, and $M$ is simply connected. The fields $$h=g+N^{-1}X^\\flat\\otimes X^\\flat,\n \\qquad \\lambda=\\sqrt N,\\qquad \\mathcal A=N^{-1}X^\\flat\n \\label{geo-quotient-fields}$$ satisfy $h\\geq g$ and $\\,\\mathrm d\\mathcal A=0$, and there is a global smooth function $H$ on $M$ with $\\,\\mathrm dH=-\\mathcal A$. They obey $$\\Delta_h\\lambda=3\\lambda,\n \\qquad \\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_h\\lambda=\\lambda(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_h+3h),\n \\qquad R_h=-6.\n \\label{geo-static-equations}$$ Attaching $S$ in the regular boundary coordinates of Lemma <a href=\"#geo-boundary-collars\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-boundary-collars\">[geo-boundary-collars]</a> gives a smooth complete Riemannian manifold with compact connected nondegenerate boundary. Its underlying completion is homeomorphic to $\\Omega$, and its boundary is identified diffeomorphically with $S$. On that boundary, $$h|_{TS}=g|_{TS},\\qquad \\mathop{\\mathrm{Area}}_h(S)=\\mathop{\\mathrm{Area}}_g(S),\\qquad \\lambda=0,\n \\qquad \\partial_{\\nu_h}\\lambda=\\kappa_h,\n \\qquad \\mathrm{II}_h=0.\n \\label{geo-quotient-boundary}$$ Moreover, in the original end chart, $$h-g=O_2(r^{-2\\tau'}),\\qquad\n \\lambda-V_0=O_2(r^{1-\\tau'}),\\qquad \\frac{\\lambda}{V_0}\\longrightarrow1.\n \\label{geo-quotient-end}$$*\n\n</div>\n\n\n#### Boundary collars and the Killing identities\n\nInitially put $P=\\{N>0\\}\\subset M$. On $P$ define $h,\\lambda,\\mathcal A$ as in Equation <a href=\"#geo-quotient-fields\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-quotient-fields\">[geo-quotient-fields]</a>, and set $$C=h^{-1}=g^{-1}-u^{-2}X\\otimes X,\n \\qquad \\mathcal F=\\,\\mathrm d\\mathcal A.\n \\label{geo-C-F}$$ The tensor $C$ extends smoothly and nonnegatively to all of $M$. Direct completion of the square gives $$\\mathbf g=h-\\lambda^2(\\,\\mathrm dt-\\mathcal A)^2,\n \\qquad \\,\\mathrm dV_h=\\frac{u}{\\lambda}\\,\\mathrm dV_g.\n \\label{geo-square-completion}$$\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-positive-collars\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n\n**Lemma 94** (The end and the original boundary collar). *The end and a collar of $S$ in $M$ lie in $P$. In particular the interior zero set $Z=\\{N=0\\}\\cap M$ is compact. If $u|_S>0$, then $$\\,\\mathrm dN|_S=2\\kappa_h X^\\flat|_S,\n \\qquad N=2\\kappa_h u|_S\\,s+O(s^2),\n \\label{geo-positive-boundary-jet}$$ where $s\\geq0$ is $g$-normal distance into the domain. If $u|_S=0$, there are smooth $a$ and $W$ in this collar such that $$u=sa,\\qquad a|_S=\\kappa_h,\\qquad X=s^2W,\n \\qquad N=s^2\\bigl(a^2-s^2|W|_g^2\\bigr).\n \\label{geo-zero-boundary-jet}$$*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-positive-collars\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-positive-collars</summary>\n\n*Proof.* Since $X=u\\nu$ on $S$, the function $N$ vanishes there. The normal component of Equation <a href=\"#geo-input-killing\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-input-killing\">[geo-input-killing]</a> gives $\\langle\\nabla_\\nu X,\\nu\\rangle=-uK(\\nu,\\nu)$, and hence $$\\partial_\\nu N\n =2u\\partial_\\nu u-2u\\langle\\nabla_\\nu X,\\nu\\rangle\n =2u\\bigl(\\partial_\\nu u+K(X,\\nu)\\bigr)=2u\\kappa_h.$$ All tangential derivatives of $N$ vanish on $S$. This proves Equation <a href=\"#geo-positive-boundary-jet\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-positive-boundary-jet\">[geo-positive-boundary-jet]</a> and the positive-lapse collar assertion. If $u=0$ on $S$, then $X=0$ there and its tangential covariant derivatives vanish. The normal-normal and normal-tangential components of $\\operatorname{sym}\\nabla X=0$ give $\\nabla_\\nu X=0$ on $S$. Smooth division by $s$ and by $s^2$ gives Equation <a href=\"#geo-zero-boundary-jet\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-zero-boundary-jet\">[geo-zero-boundary-jet]</a>; the boundary lapse equation gives $a|_S=\\kappa_h$. Compactness makes the collars uniform. Finally, Equation <a href=\"#geo-input-end\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-input-end\">[geo-input-end]</a> gives $N=V_0^2(1+O_2(r^{-\\tau'}))$, so the entire sufficiently distant end lies in $P$. The remaining zero set is a closed subset of a compact set separated from $S$. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-killing-identities\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n**Lemma 95** (Norm and twist identities). *Let $D_{\\alpha\\beta}=\\nabla^{\\mathbf g}_\\alpha\\xi_\\beta$, with the full Lorentzian contraction used in $|D|_{\\mathbf g}^2$. On $M$, $$\\frac1u\\operatorname{div}_g(uC\\,\\,\\mathrm dN)\n       =6N-2|D|_{\\mathbf g}^2.\n \\label{geo-norm-identity}$$ On $P$, the antisymmetric contravariant tensor $$Q^{ij}=uN C^{ik}C^{j\\ell}\\mathcal F_{k\\ell}\n \\label{geo-Q}$$ satisfies $\\nabla_iQ^{ij}=0$.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-killing-identities\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-killing-identities</summary>\n\n*Proof.* The Killing equation makes $D$ antisymmetric. Killing differentiation gives $\\Box_{\\mathbf g}\\xi_\\beta=-\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{\\mathbf g\\,\\beta\\gamma}\\xi^\\gamma$. Since $\\mathbf g(\\xi,\\xi)=-N$, it follows that $$\\Box_{\\mathbf g}N\n =-2|D|_{\\mathbf g}^2+2\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{\\mathbf g}(\\xi,\\xi)\n =-2|D|_{\\mathbf g}^2+6N.$$ In the last equality the additional term in Equation <a href=\"#geo-input-ricci\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-input-ricci\">[geo-input-ricci]</a> vanishes by $\\mu N=0$. For a stationary scalar the spatial block of $\\mathbf g^{-1}$ is $C$, and the spacetime volume density is $u\\sqrt{\\det g}$. This proves Equation <a href=\"#geo-norm-identity\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-norm-identity\">[geo-norm-identity]</a>.\n\nFor the second identity, write $\\vartheta=\\,\\mathrm dt-\\mathcal A$. The Killing one-form is $\\xi^\\flat=-\\lambda^2\\vartheta$, so $\\xi^\\flat\\wedge\\,\\mathrm d\\xi^\\flat=-\\lambda^4\\vartheta\\wedge\\mathcal F$. The differentiated Killing equation, contracted with the volume form, gives $$\\,\\mathrm d*_{\\mathbf g}(\\xi^\\flat\\wedge\\,\\mathrm d\\xi^\\flat)\n       =2*_{\\mathbf g}\\bigl(\\xi^\\flat\\wedge\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{\\mathbf g}(\\xi,\\cdot)\\bigr)\n       =0.$$ The right side vanishes because $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{\\mathbf g}(\\xi,\\cdot)$ is proportional to $\\xi^\\flat$. Evaluating the Hodge star using the unit time form $\\lambda\\vartheta$ turns the left side, up to a fixed orientation sign, into $\\,\\mathrm d(\\lambda^3 *_h\\mathcal F)$. Thus $$\\operatorname{div}_h\\bigl(\\lambda^3 C^{ik}C^{j\\ell}\n                                      \\mathcal F_{k\\ell}\\bigr)=0.$$ Use $\\lambda^3\\,\\mathrm dV_h=uN\\,\\mathrm dV_g$ to change the divergence density. The connection term on the free index of an antisymmetric two-tensor vanishes for either torsion-free connection. The resulting equation is exactly $\\nabla_iQ^{ij}=0$. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### Logarithmic control and vanishing twist\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-logarithmic-energy\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n\n**Lemma 96** (Transverse logarithmic energy). *On a neighborhood of $Z$, set $B=|X|_g$, $e=X/B$, and $T=e^\\perp$. For each smooth compactly supported cutoff $\\eta$ in that neighborhood, $$\\sup_{\\varepsilon>0}\n \\int_M u\\eta^2\\frac{|\\,\\mathrm dN|_C^2}{(N+\\varepsilon)^2}\\,\\mathrm dV_g<\\infty.\n \\label{geo-log-energy-bound}$$ In particular, $\\,\\mathrm d_T\\log N$ is locally square integrable on the positive side up to $Z$: $$\\int_P\\eta^2|\\,\\mathrm d_T\\log N|_g^2\\,\\mathrm dV_g<\\infty.\n \\label{geo-log-transverse}$$ No regularity or measure assumption on $Z$ is required.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-logarithmic-energy\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-logarithmic-energy</summary>\n\n\n*Proof.* On a sufficiently small fixed neighborhood of the compact set $Z$, both $u$ and $B$ are bounded below by positive constants. The tensor $C$ acts as the identity on $T$ and has eigenvalue $N/u^2$ in direction $e$. Smooth nonnegativity of $N$ implies $$|\\,\\mathrm dN|_g^2\\leq C_0N\n \\label{geo-quadratic-vanishing}$$ on compact subsets after slightly enlarging the neighborhood. Indeed, choose a uniform coordinate radius and a bound $L$ for $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_gN$ large enough that $|\\,\\mathrm dN|/L$ is less than that radius. Taylor’s Inequality along the negative gradient geodesic at length $|\\,\\mathrm dN|/L$ yields $0\\leq N-|\\,\\mathrm dN|^2/(2L)$.\n\n\n\nPut $n=(\\partial_t-X)/u$, and complete $e$ to a spatial orthonormal frame $e,E_1,E_2$. Since $\\xi=un+Be$, differentiation of its norm gives $$uD_{in}=-\\tfrac12N_i-BD_{ie}.$$ Writing $v_a=D_{ae}$, expansion of the temporal and spatial contractions therefore gives the exact formula $$-2|D|_{\\mathbf g}^2\n =\\frac{|\\,\\mathrm dN|_g^2}{u^2}\n   +\\frac{4B}{u^2}\\sum_{a=1}^2N_av_a\n   -\\frac{4N}{u^2}\\sum_{a=1}^2v_a^2-4D_{12}^2.\n \\label{geo-D-expansion}$$ All coefficients and the components of $D$ are bounded on the fixed neighborhood. Equations <a href=\"#geo-norm-identity\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-norm-identity\">[geo-norm-identity]</a> and <a href=\"#geo-quadratic-vanishing\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-quadratic-vanishing\">[geo-quadratic-vanishing]</a> consequently imply $$\\frac1u\\operatorname{div}_g(uC\\,\\,\\mathrm dN)\n                  \\leq C_1(N+|\\,\\mathrm d_TN|_g).\n \\label{geo-norm-upper-bound}$$ The additional cosmological term $6N$ has the harmless first order shown.\n\nMultiply Equation <a href=\"#geo-norm-upper-bound\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-norm-upper-bound\">[geo-norm-upper-bound]</a> by $u\\eta^2/(N+\\varepsilon)$ and integrate. Writing $E_\\varepsilon$ for the integral in Equation <a href=\"#geo-log-energy-bound\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-log-energy-bound\">[geo-log-energy-bound]</a>, before taking the supremum, integration by parts gives $$E_\\varepsilon\n -2\\int_M\\frac{u\\eta C(\\,\\mathrm d\\eta,\\,\\mathrm dN)}{N+\\varepsilon}\\,\\mathrm dV_g\n \\leq C_1\\int_Mu\\eta^2\\,\\mathrm dV_g\n    +C_1\\int_M\\frac{u\\eta^2|\\,\\mathrm d_TN|}{N+\\varepsilon}\\,\\mathrm dV_g.$$ Cauchy’s Inequality bounds the cutoff term by $E_\\varepsilon/4+C\\int u|\\,\\mathrm d\\eta|_C^2$, and the last term by $E_\\varepsilon/4+C\\int u\\eta^2$, because $|\\,\\mathrm d_TN|\\leq|\\,\\mathrm dN|_C$. This proves the uniform bound. Fatou’s Lemma on $P$, together with the positive lower bound for $u$, proves Equation <a href=\"#geo-log-transverse\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-log-transverse\">[geo-log-transverse]</a>. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-vanishing-twist\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n**Lemma 97** (Vanishing twist). *The form $\\mathcal A$ is closed on all of $P$.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-vanishing-twist\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-vanishing-twist</summary>\n\n\n*Proof.* Lower the free index of $Q^{kj}\\mathcal A_j$ using $g$. Direct substitution of $$\\mathcal F=N^{-1}\\,\\mathrm dX^\\flat-N^{-2}\\,\\mathrm dN\\wedge X^\\flat,\n \\qquad C X^\\flat=(N/u^2)X$$ gives $$W_i:=g_{ik}Q^{kj}\\mathcal A_j\n  =u^{-1}\\left\\{X^j(\\,\\mathrm dX^\\flat)_{ij}\n                    -B^2(\\,\\mathrm d_T\\log N)_i\\right\\}.\n \\label{geo-twist-contraction}$$ This expression is orthogonal to $X$. At a zero of $X$ its second numerator is interpreted as $B^2\\,\\mathrm dN-\\,\\mathrm dN(X)X^\\flat$, so the identity does not require a choice of $e$ away from the neighborhood used above.\n\n\nLet $\\chi$ be a product of three nonnegative cutoffs, excluding first $Z$, then the original boundary, then infinity. Testing $\\nabla_iQ^{ij}=0$ by $\\chi\\mathcal A_j$ gives $$\\frac12\\int_P\\chi uN C^{ik}C^{j\\ell}\n                 \\mathcal F_{ij}\\mathcal F_{k\\ell}\\,\\mathrm dV_g\n       =-\\int_P\\langle W,\\,\\mathrm d\\chi\\rangle_g\\,\\mathrm dV_g.\n \\label{geo-twist-energy}$$ The integrand on the left is nonnegative.\n\nKeep the boundary and infinity cutoffs fixed. Let the first cutoff change from zero to one on $\\varepsilon<N<2\\varepsilon$, with derivative bounded by $C/\\varepsilon$. Orthogonality in Equation <a href=\"#geo-twist-contraction\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-twist-contraction\">[geo-twist-contraction]</a> makes its error bounded by $$C\\int_{\\{\\varepsilon<N<2\\varepsilon\\}}\n       \\bigl(|\\,\\mathrm d_T\\log N|+|\\,\\mathrm d_T\\log N|^2\\bigr)\\,\\mathrm dV_g$$ on a fixed compact set. This tends to zero by Lemma <a href=\"#geo-logarithmic-energy\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-logarithmic-energy\">96</a>: the shell indicators tend pointwise to zero on $P$ and are dominated by an integrable function there. The argument also applies if $Z$ has positive volume.\n\nFor the boundary cutoff use the normal coordinate $s$. If $u|_S>0$, Equation <a href=\"#geo-positive-boundary-jet\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-positive-boundary-jet\">[geo-positive-boundary-jet]</a> gives $N\\asymp s$, $X=u|_S\\nu+O(s)$, and $\\,\\mathrm d_TN=O(s)$. Thus $W$ is bounded. Its orthogonality to $X$ implies $W(\\nu)=O(s)$, so a cutoff with derivative $O(\\delta^{-1})$ on $\\delta<s<2\\delta$ has error $O(\\delta)$. If $u|_S=0$, Equation <a href=\"#geo-zero-boundary-jet\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-zero-boundary-jet\">[geo-zero-boundary-jet]</a> gives $$u\\asymp s,\\quad X=O(s^2),\\quad \\,\\mathrm dX^\\flat=O(s),\n \\quad N\\asymp s^2,\\quad \\,\\mathrm dN=O(s),$$ and Equation <a href=\"#geo-twist-contraction\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-twist-contraction\">[geo-twist-contraction]</a> gives $W=O(s^2)$, with the same conclusion.\n\nFinally, Equation <a href=\"#geo-input-end\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-input-end\">[geo-input-end]</a> gives $W=O(r^{1-2\\tau'})$ on the end. A cutoff on $R<r<2R$ has bounded hyperbolic gradient and the shell has volume $O(R^2)$. Its error is $O(R^{3-2\\tau'})$, which vanishes since $\\tau'>3/2$. Successively removing these cutoffs and using Fatou’s Lemma in Equation <a href=\"#geo-twist-energy\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-twist-energy\">[geo-twist-energy]</a> makes its nonnegative integrand vanish everywhere. Since $uN>0$ and $C$ is positive definite on $P$, one has $\\mathcal F=0$ there. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-static-on-P\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n**Lemma 98** (Static equations and connectedness). *Equations <a href=\"#geo-static-equations\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-static-equations\">[geo-static-equations]</a> hold on $P$, and $P$ is connected.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-static-on-p\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-static-on-p</summary>\n\n*Proof.* Locally write $\\mathcal A=\\,\\mathrm df$ and $T_0=t-f$. Then $\\mathbf g=h-\\lambda^2\\,\\mathrm dT_0^2$. Equation <a href=\"#geo-input-ricci\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-input-ricci\">[geo-input-ricci]</a> is vacuum on $P$. The only mixed-time Christoffel symbols of this static product are $$\\Gamma^{T_0}_{iT_0}=\\lambda^{-1}\\partial_i\\lambda,\n \\qquad \\Gamma^i_{T_0T_0}=\\lambda h^{ij}\\partial_j\\lambda.$$ Thus its spatial Ricci tensor is $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_h-\\lambda^{-1}\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_h\\lambda$, and its time-time component is $\\lambda\\Delta_h\\lambda$. Comparing with $-3\\mathbf g$ gives the first two equations in Equation <a href=\"#geo-static-equations\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-static-equations\">[geo-static-equations]</a>; tracing gives $R_h=-6$. These equations are intrinsic and hence hold globally on $P$.\n\nThe end belongs to a single component of $P$. Any other component has compact closure in the original manifold with boundary. The continuous function $\\lambda$ is zero on every finite boundary point of that component, including a possible point on $S$. It therefore attains a positive maximum at an interior point, contrary to $\\Delta_h\\lambda=3\\lambda$. There is no other component. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### Optical completeness and simple connectivity\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-optical-completeness\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n**Lemma 99** (Completeness after truncation of the ordinary end). *Equip $P$ with the optical metric $k=\\lambda^{-2}h$. All escape directions other than the ordinary end have infinite $k$-length. After truncating the ordinary end at a sufficiently large sphere, the resulting manifold with boundary is complete for its intrinsic optical distance. The same is true of each of its Riemannian covering spaces.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-optical-completeness\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-optical-completeness</summary>\n\n*Proof.* Near $Z$, smooth nonnegativity and compactness give $N\\leq C\\operatorname{dist}_g(\\cdot,Z)^2$. If $\\rho=\\operatorname{dist}_g(\\cdot,Z)$, then $|\\,\\mathrm d\\rho|_g\\leq1$ almost everywhere and $$|\\,\\mathrm d\\log\\rho|_k^2\n   =N C(\\,\\mathrm d\\log\\rho,\\,\\mathrm d\\log\\rho)\n   \\leq N\\rho^{-2}\\leq C.$$ Hence approach to $Z$ has infinite optical length. In the zero boundary lapse case the same calculation uses $s$ and $N=O(s^2)$.\n\nFor positive boundary lapse it is essential to allow arbitrary tangential motion. In the $g$-normal collar decompose $X=X^\\nu\\nu+X_T$. Since $|\\,\\mathrm ds|_g=1$, the exact inverse-metric formula is $$|\\,\\mathrm ds|_k^2\n =N\\left(1-\\frac{(X^\\nu)^2}{u^2}\\right)\n =\\frac{N}{u^2}\\bigl(N+|X_T|_g^2\\bigr)=O(s^2).\n \\label{geo-optical-arbitrary-curve}$$ Here $N\\asymp s$, $X_T=O(s)$, and $u$ is bounded below. Therefore $|\\,\\mathrm ds(v)|\\leq Cs|v|_k$ for every vector $v$, and any curve approaching $S$ has infinite optical length. This proves the assertion without restricting to normal curves.\n\nAfter truncation, $N$ is bounded above, so $k\\geq c g$. Any optical Cauchy sequence is consequently Cauchy for $g$ and has a limit in the compact original region with the large sphere attached. The logarithmic estimates exclude a limit in $Z$ or in $S$. Every other limit is an ordinary smooth point of the truncated metric, including its large-sphere boundary. This proves completeness. A smooth manifold with boundary and its intrinsic Riemannian distance is a locally compact length space; completeness makes it proper. For a covering metric completeness follows by projecting a Cauchy sequence and then taking an evenly covered small neighborhood of its limit. Sufficiently short connecting paths remain in that neighborhood, so the sequence eventually lies in a single sheet and converges there. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-null-index-obstruction\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n**Lemma 100** (Two convex faces cannot be joined by a shortest optical path). *Let $(L,h,\\lambda)$ satisfy the static equations in Equation <a href=\"#geo-static-equations\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-static-equations\">[geo-static-equations]</a>, with $\\lambda>0$. Suppose that two compact boundary faces $\\Sigma_0,\\Sigma_1$ have positive $h$-mean curvature for the normals pointing out of $L$. There is no shortest optical path between these faces which is orthogonal at its endpoints and otherwise interior.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-null-index-obstruction\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-null-index-obstruction</summary>\n\n*Proof.* Suppose such a path has optical length $\\ell>0$. In the abstract static product $(\\mathbb R\\times L,\\widehat{\\mathbf g})$, where $\\widehat{\\mathbf g}=-\\lambda^2\\,\\mathrm dT^2+h$, its lift with increasing $T$ from $0$ to $\\ell$ is a null geodesic up to reparametrization. One can see this directly from the null energy relation $\\lambda^2\\dot T=E>0$: optical arclength and affine parameter are related by $\\,\\mathrm ds/\\,\\mathrm dT=\\lambda^2/E$, and the spatial geodesic equation becomes the optical geodesic equation. Use an affine parameter on a compact interval $[a,b]$ and write its tangent as $k_0$.\n\nThis null curve has no future timelike competitor with endpoints in the fixed-time surfaces $\\{0\\}\\times\\Sigma_0$ and $\\{\\ell\\}\\times\\Sigma_1$. Indeed every such competitor satisfies $$\\ell=\\int_a^b\\dot T\\,\\,\\mathrm ds\n >\\int_a^b\\frac{|\\dot x|_h}{\\lambda}\\,\\,\\mathrm ds\n \\geq\\operatorname{dist}_{\\lambda^{-2}h}(\\Sigma_0,\\Sigma_1)=\\ell.$$ We produce a competitor by second variation.\n\nChoose a parallel orthonormal screen pair $E_1,E_2$ along the null geodesic, with $\\langle E_A,k_0\\rangle=0$, initially tangent to $\\{0\\}\\times\\Sigma_0$. At the terminal endpoint, add suitable multiples of $k_0$ to remove their time components. Orthogonality to $k_0$ then places them in $T\\Sigma_1$. Extending these multiples smoothly along the curve gives fields $V_A=E_A+b_Ak_0$ tangent to the endpoint surfaces, still orthonormal, with $\\langle\\nabla_{k_0}V_A,\\nabla_{k_0}V_A\\rangle=0$. Let $H_0,H_1>0$ denote the specified mean curvatures. The spatial component of $k_0$ is $-c_0\\nu_0$ initially and $c_1\\nu_1$ terminally, for positive $c_0,c_1$. The static time slices have zero second fundamental form. The endpoint terms in the energy second variation therefore have trace $-c_0H_0-c_1H_1$.\n\nMore explicitly, choose variations with initial and terminal curves in the fixed-time surfaces and first variational fields $V_A$. The second variation of $\\frac12\\int\\langle\\dot\\gamma,\\dot\\gamma\\rangle$ is $$I(V_A,V_A)=\n \\int_a^b\\left(\n |\\nabla_{k_0}V_A|^2\n -\\langle R(V_A,k_0)k_0,V_A\\rangle\\right)\\,\\mathrm ds\n +\\left[\\langle\\nabla_{V_A}V_A,k_0\\rangle\\right]_a^b.$$ At an endpoint, the surface acceleration has normal component $-\\mathrm{II}_{\\nu_j}(V_A,V_A)$. This proves the stated signs. Generator multiples do not change the curvature term, and summing the screen curvatures gives $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_{\\widehat{\\mathbf g}}(k_0,k_0)=0$. Consequently $$\\sum_{A=1}^2I(V_A,V_A)=-c_0H_0-c_1H_1<0.\n \\label{geo-negative-null-index}$$ Choose one of these fields with negative index and a smooth variation $\\gamma_\\varepsilon$ realizing it. The first variation of squared speed vanishes pointwise, because $\\langle\\nabla_{k_0}V,k_0\\rangle=0$. Put $q(s)=\\partial_\\varepsilon^2|\\dot\\gamma_\\varepsilon|^2|_{\\varepsilon=0}$; its integral is $2I(V,V)<0$. Let $\\overline q$ be its negative average. Choose a parallel auxiliary null vector $L_0$ with $\\langle L_0,k_0\\rangle=-1$, and add to the variation a second-order displacement $\\frac12\\varepsilon^2 f(s)L_0$, where $$f(a)=0,\\qquad f'(s)=\\tfrac12(q(s)-\\overline q).$$ Then $f(b)=0$, so the endpoints are unchanged; the second variation of squared speed changes by $-2f'$ and becomes the constant $\\overline q<0$. Uniform Taylor expansion on $[a,b]$ now makes the varied curve timelike for all sufficiently small nonzero $\\varepsilon$. It remains future directed because $\\dot T>0$ on the original compact segment. Its endpoint contacts remain transverse and directed into and out of $L$; away from small endpoint intervals the original curve lies a positive distance from the boundary. Thus the variation remains in $L$ and is the forbidden timelike competitor. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-simple-connectivity\" class=\"proposition\">\n\n**Proposition 101** (Simple connectivity of the timelike region). *The connected manifold $P$ is simply connected.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-simple-connectivity\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-simple-connectivity</summary>\n\n*Proof.* Suppose its universal cover is nontrivial. The ordinary end is a product of a sphere and a ray and is simply connected. Its inverse image therefore consists of at least two disjoint copies. Truncate every copy at the same large radius $R$. Their boundary faces are compact spheres. By Equation <a href=\"#geo-input-end\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-input-end\">[geo-input-end]</a> and the formula for $h$, their mean curvatures for the normals pointing into the removed tails satisfy $$H_h=\\frac{2\\sqrt{1+R^2}}{R}+o(1)>0.$$ The truncated cover is connected: attaching or removing a product tail cannot join different components of its complement. By Lemma <a href=\"#geo-optical-completeness\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-optical-completeness\">99</a> its intrinsic optical metric is complete and proper.\n\nFix one face. The union of all the other faces is a closed set, since it is the inverse image of the truncation sphere with the fixed component removed: local finiteness in evenly covered neighborhoods makes each component open as well as closed within that inverse image. The remaining union is disjoint from the fixed compact face. Properness implies that the positive distance between that face and the union is attained. A minimizing path has no intermediate contact with a face: a later contact with the initial face or an earlier contact with any other face would shorten the selected distance. To check its endpoint directions without assuming optical convexity, let $\\rho$ be the inward $k$-distance to the initial face in its smooth normal collar, and parametrize the path by unit optical speed from $t=0$. The bound $|d\\rho|_k=1$ gives $\\rho(\\gamma(t))\\le t$; replacing the initial segment by a normal collar segment gives the reverse inequality by minimality. Hence $\\rho(\\gamma(t))=t$ and $\\dot\\gamma=\\nabla_k\\rho$ near the endpoint. Apply the same argument backwards at the final face. The path is therefore an interior geodesic with transverse orthogonal endpoint contacts. The static equations lift to the cover, so Lemma <a href=\"#geo-null-index-obstruction\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-null-index-obstruction\">100</a> gives a contradiction. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### The geometry of a possible interior null set\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-null-leaf-equations\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n\n**Lemma 102** (Foliated coordinates and boundary-leaf equations). *There is a neighborhood of $Z$ on which $X^\\flat$ defines a smooth cooriented integrable plane field. In local foliated coordinates it has the form $$X^\\flat=B_1\\,\\mathrm dy,\\qquad B_1>0,\\qquad\n g=q_y+D_1^2\\,\\mathrm dy^2,\\qquad N=B_1a(y),\\qquad a\\geq0.\n \\label{geo-null-foliation}$$ At any leaf in the relative boundary of $P$, one has $a=a'=0$. Put $b_1=\\sqrt{B_1}$ and let $\\mathcal K_y$ denote the Gaussian curvature of $q_y$. On such a boundary leaf, $$\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_{q_y}b_1=\\tfrac12b_1(\\mathcal K_y+3)q_y,\n \\qquad \\Delta_{q_y}(b_1^2)=6b_1^2-a''.\n \\label{geo-boundary-leaf-system}$$*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-null-leaf-equations\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-null-leaf-equations</summary>\n\n*Proof.* The compactness of $Z$ and positivity of $u$ give $X\\ne0$ on a neighborhood of $Z$. On $P$, closedness of $\\mathcal A$ gives $X^\\flat\\wedge\\,\\mathrm dX^\\flat=0$. This extends by continuity to the relative boundary of $P$. In an open region where $N=0$, Equation <a href=\"#geo-D-expansion\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-D-expansion\">[geo-D-expansion]</a> and Equation <a href=\"#geo-norm-identity\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-norm-identity\">[geo-norm-identity]</a> give $D_{12}=0$. Since the spatial restriction of $\\,\\mathrm d\\xi^\\flat$ is $\\,\\mathrm dX^\\flat=2D_{ij}\\,\\mathrm dx^i\\otimes\\,\\mathrm dx^j$ in components, the restriction of $\\,\\mathrm dX^\\flat$ to $X^\\perp$ vanishes there also. These cases exhaust the neighborhood, proving Frobenius integrability.\n\nChoose the transverse coordinate oriented so that $X^\\flat=B_1\\,\\mathrm dy$ with $B_1>0$, and transport coordinates within the leaves orthogonally using $g$. This gives the metric decomposition in Equation <a href=\"#geo-null-foliation\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-null-foliation\">[geo-null-foliation]</a>. On the positive set, $\\,\\mathrm d(B_1\\,\\mathrm dy/N)=0$ says that every leaf derivative of $N/B_1$ vanishes. The same derivatives vanish on the interior of the zero set and, by continuity, on its remaining boundary. Thus $N/B_1=a(y)$ throughout the coordinate neighborhood. Nonnegativity gives $a=a'=0$ at a zero. A boundary leaf is approached by leaves with $a>0$.\n\nWe compute the limit of the static equations from those positive leaves. On them, $$h=q_y+P_1^2\\,\\mathrm dy^2,\\qquad\n P_1=\\left(D_1^2+\\frac{B_1}{a}\\right)^{1/2},\n \\qquad \\lambda=b_1\\sqrt a.$$ The second fundamental form of a leaf in $h$ is $k_{AB}=(2P_1)^{-1}\\partial_yq_{AB}=O(\\sqrt a)$, and $P_1^{-1}\\partial_yk_{AB}=O(a+|a'|)$. The tangential Ricci formula is therefore $$(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Ric}}_h)_{AB}\n  =\\mathcal K_y q_{AB}-P_1^{-1}(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_{q_y}P_1)_{AB}\n        +O(a+|a'|)\n  \\longrightarrow\n  \\mathcal K_y q_{AB}-b_1^{-1}(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_{q_y}b_1)_{AB}.$$ The tangential normalized Hessian has the limit $$\\lambda^{-1}(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_h\\lambda)_{AB}\n =b_1^{-1}(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_{q_y}b_1)_{AB}+O(a+|a'|)\n \\longrightarrow b_1^{-1}(\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_{q_y}b_1)_{AB}.$$ These estimates follow directly by inserting $P_1=b_1a^{-1/2}\n(1+aD_1^2/B_1)^{1/2}$; all coefficients in their error terms are bounded smooth functions on a fixed coordinate patch. The tangential static Ricci equation gives the first equation in Equation <a href=\"#geo-boundary-leaf-system\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-boundary-leaf-system\">[geo-boundary-leaf-system]</a>.\n\nFor the scalar equation let $v=\\sqrt{\\det q_y}$, $f=\\log b_1$, and $w=(1+aD_1^2/B_1)^{1/2}$. The normal divergence contribution to $\\lambda^{-1}\\Delta_h\\lambda$ is exactly $$\\frac1{b_1^2wv}\\partial_y\n       \\left[vw^{-1}\\left(af_y+\\frac{a'}2\\right)\\right].\n \\label{geo-normal-laplacian-limit}$$ At $a=a'=0$ it tends to $a''/(2b_1^2)$. The tangential contribution tends to $\\Delta_{q_y}b_1/b_1+|\\,\\mathrm db_1|_{q_y}^2/b_1^2$. Hence $\\Delta_h\\lambda=3\\lambda$ gives $$b_1\\Delta_{q_y}b_1+|\\,\\mathrm db_1|_{q_y}^2+\\frac{a''}2=3b_1^2,$$ which is the second equation in Equation <a href=\"#geo-boundary-leaf-system\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-boundary-leaf-system\">[geo-boundary-leaf-system]</a>. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### Exclusion of flat boundary null leaves\n\nHere a boundary null leaf is called flat when $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_gN=0$ along it, equivalently when $a''(y_0)=0$ in Equation <a href=\"#geo-null-foliation\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-null-foliation\">[geo-null-foliation]</a>. We exclude these leaves first; the remaining null leaves are then ruled out in Proposition <a href=\"#geo-no-null-set\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-no-null-set\">105</a>.\n\nWe first give the elementary orbitwise construction needed at a possibly singular compact invariant set. The construction produces an arc through each point separately and requires no manifold structure on that set.\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-flat-fast-arc\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n\n**Lemma 103** (A transverse arc with fast backward decay). *Let $\\phi_t$ be a smooth complete flow on a smooth Riemannian three-manifold $(M,g)$, and let $\\mathcal K\\subset M$ be a compact set invariant for all $t\\in\\mathbb R$. Suppose that a smooth nonvanishing one-form $\\alpha$ is defined near $\\mathcal K$, that $E=\\ker\\alpha$ is preserved by the differential of the flow along $\\mathcal K$, and that, for every $p\\in\\mathcal K$, $t\\geq0$, and $v\\in E_p$, $$\\label{geo-flat-rate-hypotheses}\n \\lvert v\\rvert_g\\leq\n \\lvert D\\phi_t(p)v\\rvert_g\\leq e^t\\lvert v\\rvert_g,\n \\qquad\n \\alpha_{\\phi_t(p)}\\circ D\\phi_t(p)=e^{2t}\\alpha_p.$$ There are constants $\\epsilon,C>0$ such that every $p\\in\\mathcal K$ admits a $C^1$ embedded arc $\\gamma_p:(-\\epsilon,\\epsilon)\\longrightarrow M$ with $$\\label{geo-flat-arc-conclusion}\n \\gamma_p(0)=p,\\qquad\n \\alpha_p(\\gamma_p'(0))=1,\\qquad\n d_g\\bigl(\\phi_{-t}(\\gamma_p(\\xi)),\\phi_{-t}(p)\\bigr)\n \\leq C\\lvert\\xi\\rvert e^{-3t/2}\\quad(t\\geq0).$$ By decreasing $\\epsilon$, all the backward arcs can be kept in any prescribed neighborhood of $\\mathcal K$. No regularity of the family $p\\mapsto\\gamma_p$ is asserted or needed.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-flat-fast-arc\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-flat-fast-arc</summary>\n\n\n*Proof.* *An invariant transverse line.* Write $f=\\phi_1$ and use the smooth complementary vector $$\\nu_p=\\frac{\\alpha_p^\\sharp}{\\lvert\\alpha_p\\rvert_g^2},\n \\qquad \\alpha_p(\\nu_p)=1.$$ Relative to $T_pM=E_p\\oplus\\mathbb R\\nu_p$, the forward derivative has the block form $$\\label{geo-flat-forward-blocks}\n Df_p=\n \\begin{pmatrix} A_p&B_p\\\\0&e^2\\end{pmatrix},\n \\qquad \\lVert A_p\\rVert\\leq e.$$ Here $B_p\\in E_{f(p)}$ and $\\sup_{\\mathcal K}\\lvert B_p\\rvert_g<\\infty$. Fix a full orbit $p_n=f^n(p)$, $n\\in\\mathbb Z$. A transverse line at $p_n$ with generator $\\nu_{p_n}+v_n$, $v_n\\in E_{p_n}$, is invariant precisely when its slopes satisfy $$\\label{geo-flat-slope-recurrence}\n v_{n+1}=e^{-2}(A_{p_n}v_n+B_{p_n}).$$ Each affine map in this recurrence contracts differences by at most $e^{-1}$. Starting with slope zero at $p_{n-k}$ and letting $k\\to\\infty$ therefore gives a bounded solution at $p_n$; the solutions at different indices obey the same recurrence. Equivalently, one may sum the absolutely convergent series obtained by repeated substitution. Its bound is $$\\label{geo-flat-slope-bound}\n \\sup_{n\\in\\mathbb Z}\\lvert v_n\\rvert_g\n \\leq\\frac{\\sup_{\\mathcal K}\\lvert B\\rvert_g}{e^2-e}.$$ The bounded solution is unique: the difference of two such solutions at index $n$ is at most $e^{-k}$ times their uniformly bounded difference at index $n-k$.\n\nSet $u_n=\\nu_{p_n}+v_n$ and $U_n=\\mathbb R u_n$. Then $$\\alpha_{p_n}(u_n)=1,\\qquad Df_{p_n}u_n=e^2u_{n+1}.$$ Compactness, nonvanishing of $\\alpha$, and Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-slope-bound\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-slope-bound\">[geo-flat-slope-bound]</a> give uniform equivalence between the ambient norm and the norm $$\\lvert(s,w)\\rvert_n=\\max\\{\\lvert s\\rvert,\\lvert w\\rvert_g\\},\n \\qquad su_n+w\\in U_n\\oplus E_{p_n}.$$ In particular these transverse lines have angles uniformly bounded away from zero relative to $E$.\n\n\n\n\n*Uniform charts and backward products.* Put $q_j=p_{-j}$ for $j\\geq0$. Choose centered charts $$\\Psi_j(s,w)=\\exp_{q_j}(s u_{-j}+w),\\qquad w\\in E_{q_j}.$$ They and their inverses have uniformly bounded derivatives on suitable fixed radii. This follows from compactness and the uniformly bounded linear coordinate changes just constructed. No derivatives of $U_n$ as a function of $p_n$ are used. On a fixed smaller radius $\\rho>0$, the backward time-one maps in these charts have the form $$\\label{geo-flat-backward-maps}\n \\Psi_{j+1}^{-1}\\circ\\phi_{-1}\\circ\\Psi_j(z)\n =\\begin{pmatrix}c&0\\\\0&T_j\\end{pmatrix}z+R_j(z),\n \\qquad c=e^{-2},$$ where $T_j=D\\phi_{-1}|_{E_{q_j}}$ maps $E_{q_j}$ onto $E_{q_{j+1}}$. The remainders satisfy, in the displayed norms, $$\\label{geo-flat-remainders}\n R_j(0)=0,\\qquad DR_j(0)=0,\\qquad\n \\sup_{j\\geq0,\\,\\lvert z\\rvert\\leq\\rho}\n \\lVert D^2R_j(z)\\rVert\\leq M_0$$ for some finite $M_0$. We increase $M_0$ to a positive number if necessary. Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-rate-hypotheses\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-rate-hypotheses\">[geo-flat-rate-hypotheses]</a> gives $$\\label{geo-flat-inverse-products}\n \\bigl\\lVert T_j^{-1}T_{j+1}^{-1}\\cdots T_i^{-1}\\bigr\\rVert\n \\leq e^{i-j+1}\\qquad(i\\geq j).$$ Indeed that product is the forward leaf derivative from $q_{i+1}$ to $q_j$.\n\n\n*The two Green sums.* Fix $\\beta=3/2$ and consider the Banach space of sequences $z_j=(s_j,w_j)\\in\\mathbb R\\oplus E_{q_j}$ with norm $$\\lVert z\\rVert_\\beta\n =\\sup_{j\\geq0}e^{\\beta j}\\max\\{\\lvert s_j\\rvert,\\lvert w_j\\rvert_g\\}.$$ For a forcing sequence $r_j=(r_j^s,r_j^E)$ taking values in $\\mathbb R\\oplus E_{q_{j+1}}$, use the analogous norm with weight $e^{\\beta j}$. Define $$\\begin{aligned}\n\\label{geo-flat-green-sums}\n (Gr)^s_j\n &=\\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}c^{j-1-i}r_i^s,\\\\\n (Gr)^E_j\n &=-\\sum_{i=j}^{\\infty}\n T_j^{-1}T_{j+1}^{-1}\\cdots T_i^{-1}r_i^E.\n \\notag\n\\end{aligned}$$ The first sum is empty when $j=0$. Both sums converge in the indicated weighted norm. More generally, for $1<\\beta<2$, $$\\label{geo-flat-green-bound}\n \\lVert G\\rVert\\leq\\Gamma_\\beta,\n \\qquad\n \\Gamma_\\beta=\\max\\left\\{\n \\frac{e^\\beta}{1-e^{\\beta-2}},\\,\n \\frac{e}{1-e^{1-\\beta}}\\right\\}.$$ For the first sum, setting $k=j-1-i$ bounds its weighted norm by $e^\\beta\\sum_{k\\geq0}e^{(\\beta-2)k}\\lVert r\\rVert_\\beta$. For the second, Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-inverse-products\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-inverse-products\">[geo-flat-inverse-products]</a> gives the bound $e\\sum_{k\\geq0}e^{(1-\\beta)k}\\lVert r\\rVert_\\beta$.\n\n\n\nPrescribe a small initial transverse coordinate $\\xi\\in\\mathbb R$ and put $\\mathcal H(\\xi)_j=(c^j\\xi,0)$. The desired orbit sequence is a fixed point of $$\\label{geo-flat-fixed-point}\n z=\\mathcal H(\\xi)+G\\mathcal R(z),\\qquad\n \\mathcal R(z)_j=R_j(z_j).$$ Choose $0<\\delta<\\rho$ so small that $$\\label{geo-flat-parameter-choice}\n \\vartheta_0:=\\Gamma_\\beta M_0\\delta\\leq\\tfrac12,\n \\qquad \\lvert\\xi\\rvert\\leq\\tfrac12\\delta.$$ On the closed ball $\\lVert z\\rVert_\\beta\\leq\\delta$, Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-remainders\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-remainders\">[geo-flat-remainders]</a> yields $$\\lVert\\mathcal R(z)\\rVert_\\beta\\leq\\tfrac12 M_0\\delta^2,\n \\qquad\n \\lVert\\mathcal R(z)-\\mathcal R(\\widetilde z)\\rVert_\\beta\n \\leq M_0\\delta\\lVert z-\\widetilde z\\rVert_\\beta.$$ Consequently the right side of Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-fixed-point\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-fixed-point\">[geo-flat-fixed-point]</a> maps that ball into its ball of radius $3\\delta/4$ and contracts distances by at most $\\vartheta_0$. The contraction principle gives a unique fixed point there, with $$\\label{geo-flat-sequence-decay}\n \\lVert z(\\xi)\\rVert_\\beta\n \\leq\\frac{\\lvert\\xi\\rvert}{1-\\vartheta_0}\\leq2\\lvert\\xi\\rvert.$$ Substituting the sums in Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-green-sums\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-green-sums\">[geo-flat-green-sums]</a> shows that this fixed point satisfies Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-backward-maps\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-backward-maps\">[geo-flat-backward-maps]</a> at every step, with $s_0=\\xi$. It therefore represents an actual backward orbit, rather than a sequence of approximate orbit points.\n\n*Dependence on the initial coordinate.* The same contraction estimate gives $$\\lVert z(\\xi+h)-z(\\xi)\\rVert_\\beta\n \\leq\\frac{\\lvert h\\rvert}{1-\\vartheta_0}.$$ The map $\\mathcal R$ is continuously differentiable on this sequence ball: its derivative acts pointwise by $DR_j(z_j)$, and the uniform second-derivative bound in Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-remainders\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-remainders\">[geo-flat-remainders]</a> bounds the remainder in the weighted norm. In particular $\\lVert G D\\mathcal R(z(\\xi))\\rVert\\leq \\vartheta_0$. Inverting by a Neumann series gives $$\\label{geo-flat-parameter-derivative}\n Dz(\\xi)h\n =\\bigl(I-GD\\mathcal R(z(\\xi))\\bigr)^{-1}\\mathcal H(h).$$ For clarity, this is a genuine Fréchet derivative: Taylor’s estimate and the preceding Lipschitz bound give $$\\bigl\\lVert z(\\xi+h)-z(\\xi)-Dz(\\xi)h\\bigr\\rVert_\\beta\n \\leq\\frac{\\Gamma_\\beta M_0}{2(1-\\vartheta_0)^3}\\lvert h\\rvert^2.$$ The derivative is continuous by the same uniform estimates. At $\\xi=0$, the fixed point is zero and $D\\mathcal R(0)=0$, so $Dz(0)h=((c^jh,0))_{j\\geq0}$.\n\nDefine $\\gamma_p(\\xi)=\\Psi_0(z_0(\\xi))$. Its initial derivative is $u_0$, hence $\\alpha_p(\\gamma_p'(0))=1$. Since $s_0=\\xi$, it is an embedded graph in this chart on a smaller interval. Uniform comparison between chart and ambient distances, together with Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-sequence-decay\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-sequence-decay\">[geo-flat-sequence-decay]</a>, proves Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-arc-conclusion\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-arc-conclusion\">[geo-flat-arc-conclusion]</a> at integer times. The smooth flow has uniformly bounded derivatives near $\\mathcal K$ for times in $[-1,0]$; decreasing the chart radius if necessary gives the same estimate for all intervening times. Compactness makes all constants uniform in $p$. Shrinking $\\epsilon$ then keeps the whole backward arc in any prescribed neighborhood of $\\mathcal K$. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-flat-exclusion\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n\n**Lemma 104** (Flat boundary null leaves cannot occur). *Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth three-dimensional Riemannian manifold and let $N\\in C^\\infty(M)$ be nonnegative, with compact zero set $Z=\\{N=0\\}$. Put $P=\\{N>0\\}$, with boundary taken in $M$. Suppose a neighborhood $U$ of $Z$ carries a smooth nonvanishing one-form $\\alpha$ defining a cooriented foliation by two-dimensional leaves. Assume that every sufficiently small foliated chart can be written as $$\\label{geo-flat-factorization}\n \\alpha=B\\,\\mathrm dy,\\qquad B>0,\\qquad\n N=B\\,a(y),\\qquad a\\geq0,$$ with smooth coefficients. Let $q$ be the induced metric on a plaque $\\Sigma=\\{y=y_0\\}\\subset\\partial P$, let $K_\\Sigma$ be its Gaussian curvature, and put $b=\\sqrt B$. Suppose the following leaf equations hold on every such plaque: $$\\label{geo-flat-leaf-equations}\n \\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_\\Sigma b=\\tfrac12 b(K_\\Sigma+3)q,\n \\qquad\n \\Delta_\\Sigma(b^2)=6b^2-a''(y_0).$$ Then $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_gN(p)\\ne0$ for every $p\\in\\partial P$. Equivalently, every boundary zero in Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-factorization\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-factorization\">[geo-flat-factorization]</a> satisfies $a''(y_0)>0$.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-flat-exclusion\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-flat-exclusion</summary>\n\n*Proof.* *The intrinsic vector field and the compact flat set.* On a foliated chart define $$f=\\log b,\\qquad Y=\\nabla_\\Sigma f,\\qquad L=\\lvert Y\\rvert_g^2.$$ On an overlap of cooriented charts the transverse coordinates satisfy $\\widetilde y=\\vartheta(y)$ with $\\vartheta'>0$ after restriction to an overlap plaque. Consequently $$\\widetilde B=\\frac{B}{\\vartheta'(y)},\\qquad\n \\log\\sqrt{\\widetilde B}\n =\\log\\sqrt B-\\tfrac12\\log\\vartheta'(y).$$ The last term has zero leaf derivative. Thus $Y$ and $L$ are globally defined smooth fields on $U$, even though $f$ need not be a global function. The vector field $Y$ is tangent to the foliation.\n\n\nAt a zero $y_0$ of $a$, nonnegativity gives $a'(y_0)=0$, and direct differentiation of Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-factorization\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-factorization\">[geo-flat-factorization]</a> gives $$\\label{geo-flat-hessian-zero}\n \\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_gN=B\\,a''(y_0)\\,\\mathrm dy\\otimes\\mathrm dy\n \\quad\\hbox{on the plaque }\\{y=y_0\\}.$$ In particular flatness, meaning $a''(y_0)=0$, is independent of the chosen transverse coordinate. The boundary property is also constant along a plaque: $N>0$ on that chart exactly where $a(y)>0$. The set $$\\label{geo-flat-compact-flat-set}\n F=\\partial P\\cap\\{\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_gN=0\\}$$ is therefore closed in $Z$, compact, and locally a union of whole plaques. It is preserved by the local flow of $Y$.\n\nChoose a neighborhood $U_0$ of $Z$ with compact closure in $U$ and multiply $Y$ by a smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\\overline{U_0}$. Extend the resulting field by zero to $M$ and denote its complete flow by $\\phi_t$. Compact support ensures completeness. On $F$ this flow agrees with the original leafwise flow for all times: local plaque invariance and closedness of $F$ show that $\\{t:\\phi_t(p)\\in F\\}$ is both open and closed in $\\mathbb R$ for every $p\\in F$. In all subsequent uses outside $F$ we keep the flow inside $U_0$, where the cutoff equals one.\n\n\n*The logistic identity.* On a flat plaque, tracing the first equation in Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-leaf-equations\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-leaf-equations\">[geo-flat-leaf-equations]</a> gives $\\Delta_\\Sigma b=b(K_\\Sigma+3)$. The second then gives $$6b^2=\\Delta_\\Sigma(b^2)\n =2b^2(K_\\Sigma+3)+2\\lvert\\mathrm d_\\Sigma b\\rvert_q^2.$$ It follows that $$\\label{geo-flat-logistic-identities}\n K_\\Sigma=-L,\\qquad\n \\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_\\Sigma f=\\frac{3-L}{2}q-\n \\mathrm d_\\Sigma f\\otimes\\mathrm d_\\Sigma f,\n \\qquad Y(L)=3L(1-L).$$ For the last identity, use $Y(L)=2\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_\\Sigma f(Y,Y)$.\n\nSince $F$ is compact and invariant, $L$ is bounded on every complete orbit in $F$. A logistic solution with $L(0)>1$ has the explicit form $$L(t)=\\frac{L(0)e^{3t}}{1-L(0)+L(0)e^{3t}}$$ and blows up in finite negative time. Thus $0\\leq L\\leq1$ on $F$. Suppose for contradiction that $F$ is nonempty. On any flat plaque $L$ cannot vanish identically: that would give $Y=0$ and $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_\\Sigma f=0$, whereas Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-logistic-identities\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-logistic-identities\">[geo-flat-logistic-identities]</a> would give $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_\\Sigma f=\\tfrac32 q$. Hence some point of $F$ has $L>0$. The forward logistic orbit through this point has $L(t)\\to1$. Compactness supplies an accumulation point with $L=1$, so $$\\label{geo-flat-unit-set}\n F_1=F\\cap\\{L=1\\}$$ is a nonempty compact set invariant under the full flow.\n\n\n*Leaf and transverse derivative rates.* Along $F_1$, Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-logistic-identities\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-logistic-identities\">[geo-flat-logistic-identities]</a> becomes $$\\label{geo-flat-unit-hessian}\n \\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_\\Sigma f=q-\\mathrm d_\\Sigma f\\otimes\\mathrm d_\\Sigma f,\n \\qquad \\lvert Y\\rvert_g=1.$$ For a leaf-tangent vector $v(t)=D\\phi_t(p)v(0)$, $p\\in F_1$, the usual derivative of its squared length within the leaf is $$\\frac{\\mathrm d}{\\mathrm dt}\\lvert v(t)\\rvert_g^2\n =2\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_\\Sigma f(v(t),v(t))\n =2\\bigl(\\lvert v(t)\\rvert_g^2-\n             \\langle Y,v(t)\\rangle_g^2\\bigr).$$ This lies between zero and $2\\lvert v(t)\\rvert_g^2$. Integration gives the two tangent inequalities in Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-rate-hypotheses\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-rate-hypotheses\">[geo-flat-rate-hypotheses]</a>. Furthermore, throughout $U_0$, tangency of $Y$ implies $Y(y)=0$ and $$\\label{geo-flat-alpha-and-n-evolution}\n \\mathcal L_Y\\alpha=Y(B)\\,\\mathrm dy=2L\\alpha,\n \\qquad Y(N)=2LN.$$ Here $Y(\\log B)=2Y(f)=2L$; the second identity also holds where $N=0$, by the smooth factorization. Since $L=1$ along $F_1$, the first identity gives $\\alpha_{\\phi_t(p)}\\circ D\\phi_t(p)=e^{2t}\\alpha_p$. All hypotheses of Lemma <a href=\"#geo-flat-fast-arc\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-fast-arc\">103</a> therefore hold with $\\mathcal K=F_1$ and $E=\\ker\\alpha$.\n\n\n*The two incompatible decay bounds.* Fix $p\\in F_1$ and apply Lemma <a href=\"#geo-flat-fast-arc\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-fast-arc\">103</a>. By compactness and continuity choose a neighborhood $V$ of $F_1$, with closure in $U_0$, on which $L\\leq5/4$. Shrink the resulting transverse arc so that all its backward trajectories remain in $V$. If one of its points $q=\\gamma_p(\\xi)$ had $N(q)>0$, the second equation in Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-alpha-and-n-evolution\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-alpha-and-n-evolution\">[geo-flat-alpha-and-n-evolution]</a> would give, for every $t\\geq0$, $$\\label{geo-flat-n-lower-bound}\n N(\\phi_{-t}(q))\n =N(q)\\exp\\left(-\\int_0^t2L(\\phi_{-s}(q))\\,\\mathrm ds\\right)\n \\geq N(q)e^{-5t/2}.$$ In particular the trajectory remains positive at each finite time.\n\n\nOn the other hand, $N$ and $\\mathrm dN$ vanish at every point of $F_1$, because $N$ is smooth and nonnegative. Its Hessian is uniformly bounded on a compact neighborhood of $F_1$. Taylor’s Theorem in uniform normal-coordinate balls therefore gives $$0\\leq N(x)\\leq C_0d_g(x,z)^2\n \\quad\\text{when }z\\in F_1\\text{ and }x\\text{ is sufficiently close to }z.$$ Apply this with $z=\\phi_{-j}(p)$, $x=\\phi_{-j}(q)$ and use Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-arc-conclusion\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-arc-conclusion\">[geo-flat-arc-conclusion]</a>. Uniformly for all integers $j\\geq0$, $$\\label{geo-flat-n-upper-bound}\n N(\\phi_{-j}(q))\\leq C_1\\lvert\\xi\\rvert^2e^{-3j}.$$ Equations <a href=\"#geo-flat-n-lower-bound\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-n-lower-bound\">[geo-flat-n-lower-bound]</a> and <a href=\"#geo-flat-n-upper-bound\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-n-upper-bound\">[geo-flat-n-upper-bound]</a> imply $N(q)\\leq C_1\\lvert\\xi\\rvert^2e^{-j/2}$ for every $j$, a contradiction. Thus $N$ vanishes on the whole small arc.\n\nIn a foliated chart at $p$, transversality gives $\\frac{\\mathrm d}{\\mathrm d\\xi}y(\\gamma_p(\\xi))|_{\\xi=0}\\ne0$. After restriction, the transverse coordinate of the arc covers an open interval containing $y(p)$. Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-factorization\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-factorization\">[geo-flat-factorization]</a> and positivity of $B$ then imply that $a$ vanishes on that interval. This gives an open neighborhood of $p$ on which $N=0$, contradicting $p\\in\\partial P$. Hence $F$ is empty. Finally $a''\\geq0$ at any zero of the nonnegative function $a$, so Equation <a href=\"#geo-flat-hessian-zero\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-hessian-zero\">[geo-flat-hessian-zero]</a> proves the stated strict positivity at every boundary zero. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-no-null-set\" class=\"proposition\">\n\n**Proposition 105** (No interior null set). *One has $Z=\\varnothing$, and hence $P=M$.*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-no-null-set\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-no-null-set</summary>\n\n*Proof.* Apply Lemma <a href=\"#geo-flat-exclusion\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-flat-exclusion\">104</a> with $\\alpha=X^\\flat$; its hypotheses are precisely the compactness in Lemma <a href=\"#geo-positive-collars\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-positive-collars\">94</a> and the factorization and equations in Lemma <a href=\"#geo-null-leaf-equations\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-null-leaf-equations\">102</a>. Every boundary zero therefore satisfies $a''>0$. It is therefore an isolated zero in the transverse coordinate, and its neighborhood consists of a smooth two-sided zero leaf with $P$ on both sides. There can be no open null region. Indeed, if the interior of $Z$ were nonempty, it would have a boundary in the connected manifold $M$, since $P$ is nonempty. Such a boundary point lies in $\\partial P$ and would have the just-described neighborhood with no open zero region, a contradiction. Thus all of $Z$ equals $\\partial P$, and it is a compact embedded hypersurface. The local isolation and compactness give only finitely many components. The nonvanishing global form $X^\\flat$ coorients each of them.\n\nOn a component of $Z$, the local positive functions $B_1/a''$ patch to a global smooth function. To check this, another oriented transverse coordinate has the form $\\widetilde y=\\phi(y)$ with $\\phi'>0$. At a zero leaf, $$\\widetilde B_1=B_1/\\phi',\\qquad\n \\widetilde a=\\phi'a,\\qquad\n \\widetilde a''=a''/\\phi',$$ where the last derivatives use $\\widetilde y$ and $a=a'=0$. The quotient is therefore invariant. Since $a''$ is constant along each plaque, Equation <a href=\"#geo-boundary-leaf-system\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-boundary-leaf-system\">[geo-boundary-leaf-system]</a> gives $$\\Delta_{q_y}\\left(\\frac{B_1}{a''}\\right)\n                 =6\\frac{B_1}{a''}-1.$$ The maximum and minimum principles on the compact component imply $B_1/a''=1/6$. Its leaf derivative is zero; thus $b_1$ is constant along each plaque, and the first equation in Equation <a href=\"#geo-boundary-leaf-system\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-boundary-leaf-system\">[geo-boundary-leaf-system]</a> gives $\\mathcal K_y=-3$.\n\nCut the original manifold along these finitely many two-sided components and truncate its ordinary end. The resulting compact orientable three-manifold $L$ is connected and has interior homotopy equivalent to $P$: the end and each of the original and cut boundary collars are product collars, which may be shortened without changing homotopy type. Proposition <a href=\"#geo-simple-connectivity\" data-reference-type=\"ref\" data-reference=\"geo-simple-connectivity\">101</a> therefore gives $H_1(L;\\mathbb Z)=H^1(L;\\mathbb Z)=0$. Poincaré–Lefschetz duality and the boundary long exact sequence give $$H_2(L,\\partial L;\\mathbb Z)\\cong H^1(L;\\mathbb Z)=0,\n \\qquad\n 0=H_2(L,\\partial L;\\mathbb Z)\\longrightarrow\n H_1(\\partial L;\\mathbb Z)\\longrightarrow H_1(L;\\mathbb Z)=0.$$ Consequently every component of the orientable boundary is a sphere. In particular each cut copy of a component of $Z$ is a sphere, incompatible with its constant Gaussian curvature $-3$ by Gauss–Bonnet. Thus $Z$ must have been empty. ◻\n\n</details>\n\n\n#### The regular boundary of the quotient\n\n\n<div id=\"geo-static-collar\" class=\"lemma\">\n\n\n\n\n**Lemma 106** (Static boundary collars and the time primitive). *<span id=\"geo-boundary-collars\" label=\"geo-boundary-collars\"></span> The metric $h$ has the regular completion at $S$ stated in Equation <a href=\"#geo-quotient-boundary\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-quotient-boundary\">[geo-quotient-boundary]</a>. If $u|_S=0$, its boundary structure is the original smooth boundary structure and $\\mathcal A$ extends smoothly to $S$. If $u|_S>0$, use $N$ as the original defining function and use $\\lambda=\\sqrt N$ as the quotient defining function. The quotient metric extends smoothly by reflection $\\lambda\\mapsto-\\lambda$; its diagonal blocks are even and mixed block odd. In the original collar, $$\\mathcal A=\\frac1{2\\kappa_h}\\,\\mathrm d\\log N+\\beta,\n \\qquad \\beta\\text{ is smooth and closed up to }S.\n \\label{geo-positive-A-collar}$$ In quotient normal distance $\\rho$ from $S$, both cases satisfy $$h=\\,\\mathrm d\\rho^2+q_0+O(\\rho^2),\\qquad\n \\lambda=\\kappa_h\\rho+O(\\rho^3),\n \\label{geo-normal-boundary-jets}$$ with smooth one-sided coefficients. For a global primitive $\\,\\mathrm dH=-\\mathcal A$, one has, respectively, $$H\\text{ smooth up to }S,\n \\qquad\\text{or}\\qquad\n H=-\\frac1{2\\kappa_h}\\log N+B_0,\n \\quad B_0\\text{ smooth up to }S.\n \\label{geo-time-collar}$$*\n\n</div>\n\n<details id=\"proof-stmt-geo-static-collar\"><summary>Proof of stmt-geo-static-collar</summary>\n\n*Proof.* In the zero-lapse case put $d=a^2-s^2|W|_g^2$ in Equation <a href=\"#geo-zero-boundary-jet\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-zero-boundary-jet\">[geo-zero-boundary-jet]</a>. Then $$h=g+s^2d^{-1}W^\\flat\\otimes W^\\flat,\n \\qquad \\lambda=s\\sqrt d,\n \\qquad \\mathcal A=d^{-1}W^\\flat,\n \\qquad d|_S=\\kappa_h^2.$$ These are smooth in the original collar and give $h|_{TS}=g|_{TS}$ and $\\partial_{\\nu_h}\\lambda=\\kappa_h$. The static Hessian equation extends to $S$ and gives $\\mathop{\\mathrm{Hess}}_h\\lambda=0$ there. Its tangential restriction is $\\kappa_h\\mathrm{II}_h$, proving $\\mathrm{II}_h=0$.\n\nIf $u|_S>0$, Equation <a href=\"#geo-positive-boundary-jet\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-positive-boundary-jet\">[geo-positive-boundary-jet]</a> makes $N$ a smooth original defining function. In coordinates $(N,y^1,y^2)$, smooth division of the tangential components gives $$X^\\flat=a_0(N,y)\\,\\mathrm dN+N\\beta_A(N,y)\\,\\mathrm dy^A,\n \\qquad a_0(0,y)=\\frac1{2\\kappa_h}.$$ The change $N=\\lambda^2$ gives the metric coefficients $$\\begin{aligned}\n h_{\\lambda\\lambda}&=4\\lambda^2g_{NN}+4a_0^2,\n &h_{\\lambda A}&=2\\lambda(g_{NA}+a_0\\beta_A),\n &h_{AB}&=g_{AB}+\\lambda^2\\beta_A\\beta_B,\n \\label{geo-even-odd-collar}\n\\end{aligned}$$ with the coefficients on the right evaluated at $(\\lambda^2,y)$. They are smooth across $\\lambda=0$ with the stated parity. At zero the normal block is $\\kappa_h^{-2}$, the mixed block vanishes, and the tangential block is $g|_{TS}$, so this is a nondegenerate smooth Riemannian extension. Reflection is an isometry; its fixed hypersurface is totally geodesic. The normal derivative of $\\lambda$ is $\\kappa_h$. In either case, quotient Gaussian coordinates and $\\mathrm{II}_h=0$ give $\\partial_\\rho q_\\rho|_0=0$. The static equation gives $\\partial_\\rho^2\\lambda|_0=0$, proving Equation <a href=\"#geo-normal-boundary-jets\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-normal-boundary-jets\">[geo-normal-boundary-jets]</a>.\n\nSince $a_0-(2\\kappa_h)^{-1}$ vanishes at $N=0$, division by $N$ also gives Equation <a href=\"#geo-positive-A-collar\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"geo-positive-A-collar\">[geo-positive-A-collar]</a>. Its remainder is closed by $\\,\\mathrm d\\mathcal A=0$ in the interior and smoothness at the boundary.
